name: Dooky Chase's Restaurant
tagline: Leah Chase's Creole dining room, where the civil rights movement ate.
description: Opened in 1941 and turned into an institution by the late Leah Chase, Dooky Chase's fed civil rights organizers upstairs when integrated meetings were illegal in Louisiana. The gumbo z'herbes, fried chicken and the family's art collection are all still here.

name: Willie Mae's Scotch House
tagline: Fried chicken worth the line in Tremé.
description: Willie Mae Seaton's Tremé kitchen built a national reputation on one dish. Rebuilt by volunteers after Katrina and still run by her family, it remains the fried chicken every visitor is sent to.

name: Li'l Dizzy's Cafe
tagline: Tremé Creole soul food and the buffet locals plan their week around.
description: The Baquet family's Esplanade Avenue cafe serves trout Baquet, gumbo and fried chicken to a room that mixes neighbors, politicians and musicians. A Creole restaurant lineage that runs generations deep in this city.

name: Cafe Reconcile
tagline: Creole lunch counter that doubles as a youth culinary training program.
description: On Oretha Castle Haley Boulevard, Cafe Reconcile serves red beans, smothered turkey necks and shrimp Creole while training young people from the surrounding neighborhoods for careers in hospitality. Eating here funds the program.

name: Neyow's Creole Cafe
tagline: Mid-City Creole with a fried seafood platter that arrives heavy.
description: A Bienville Street dining room known for barbecue shrimp, fried seafood and a room that stays loud and full. Neyow's is where locals send people who want the food without the tourist markup.

name: Dunbar's Creole Cooking
tagline: Tina Dunbar's red beans and fried chicken, back after the storm.
description: Dunbar's built its name on red beans and fried chicken before Katrina destroyed the original location. It came back and is again a working-class Creole lunch standard on Earhart.

name: Heard Dat Kitchen
tagline: Central City kitchen turning out plates far more ambitious than the room suggests.
description: Chef Jeff Heard cooks Creole with a fine-dining hand out of a small Felicity Street space — stuffed catfish, seafood-loaded pastas, and daily specials that regulars come by to hear read aloud.

name: Compère Lapin
tagline: Chef Nina Compton's Caribbean-Creole dining room in the Warehouse District.
description: Nina Compton, born in St. Lucia, built Compère Lapin around the meeting point of Caribbean cooking and New Orleans ingredients. Curried goat with sweet potato gnocchi is the dish people come back for.

name: Bywater American Bistro
tagline: Nina Compton's neighborhood room in the Bywater.
description: The looser, more local counterpart to Compère Lapin, set in a converted rice mill building. Seasonal plates, an open kitchen, and a menu that changes more often than the sign suggests.

name: Sweet Soulfood
tagline: All-vegan Southern cafeteria on North Broad.
description: A steam-table vegan soul food counter — smothered okra, candied yams, jambalaya, cornbread — that proved the format works without meat and holds a daily lunch crowd for it.

name: Café Dauphine
tagline: Lower Ninth Ward Creole restaurant, opened as a statement about the neighborhood.
description: Opened by a family that came back to the Lower Ninth Ward after Katrina, Café Dauphine serves stuffed shrimp, gumbo and Creole plates in a part of the city most restaurants never returned to.

name: Addis NOLA
tagline: Ethiopian cooking on Bayou Road from the Bahru family.
description: Biruk and Prince Lobo Bahru brought their mother's Ethiopian recipes to Bayou Road, a corridor with a long history of Black-owned businesses. Doro wat, kitfo, and an injera platter built for sharing.

name: Melba's Old School Poboys
tagline: 24-hour po'boys, laundromat and free-book wall on Elysian Fields.
description: Melba's is a po'boy shop, a laundromat, a lotto counter and a free lending library at once, open around the clock. Jane and Scott Wolfe run it as a genuine neighborhood utility as much as a restaurant.

name: Loretta's Authentic Pralines
tagline: The first Black woman to own a praline company in New Orleans.
description: Loretta Harrison built a praline business from a home kitchen into a French Quarter fixture, and the praline beignet is the item people cross town for. The family continues the operation.

name: Bennachin Restaurant
tagline: West African cooking in the French Quarter since the early nineties.
description: Founded by two women from Cameroon and The Gambia, Bennachin has served jama-jama, fried plantains and jollof on Royal Street for three decades — one of the longest-running African restaurants in the city.

name: Barrow's Catfish
tagline: A family catfish recipe running since 1943.
description: The Barrow family has been frying catfish in New Orleans since William Barrow started in 1943. The current Earhart Boulevard location keeps the same batter and the same reputation.

name: Two Sisters Kitchen
tagline: Tremé-adjacent soul food plate lunch with a porch.
description: A small kitchen near the courthouse serving smothered pork chops, red beans, greens and cornbread to a lunch crowd that has been coming for years. Order at the window, eat on the porch.

name: Vaucresson's Creole Cafe & Deli
tagline: The Creole hot sausage family that has fed Jazz Fest since it began.
description: The Vaucressons have made Creole hot sausage in New Orleans since 1899 and have had a booth at Jazz Fest since the very first one in 1970. The St. Bernard Avenue cafe is the family's own storefront.

name: McHardy's Chicken & Fixin'
tagline: Fried chicken by the box on North Broad.
description: A take-out counter that sells fried chicken in volume — whole boxes, sides by the pound — and has been the default order for family gatherings on that side of the city for years.

name: Sammy's Food Service & Deli
tagline: Gentilly plate lunches and a catering operation that feeds the neighborhood.
description: A Elysian Fields deli and caterer doing daily plate lunches — stuffed peppers, fried seafood, red beans — plus the catering trays that show up at a lot of New Orleans funerals and celebrations.

name: The Munch Factory
tagline: Chef Jordan Ruiz's contemporary Creole in Gentilly.
description: A family-run Gentilly restaurant serving Creole with a modern hand — shrimp and grits, blackened redfish, a brunch that fills the room. Started small and kept the same family running it.

name: Chef Ron's Gumbo Stop
tagline: Award-winning gumbo just over the parish line in Metairie.
description: Chef Ron Iafrate's gumbo has won the local competitions repeatedly. The restaurant is in Metairie rather than Orleans Parish, which matters for directions but not for the pot.

name: Fritai
tagline: Haitian cooking from chef Charly Pierre.
description: Charly Pierre cooks the Haitian food of his family — griot, pikliz, legim — in New Orleans, a city whose own Creole cooking shares a direct lineage with Haiti's. The connection is the point.

name: Queen Trini Lisa
tagline: Trinidadian doubles, roti and curry in Mid-City.
description: Chef Lisa Nelson cooks the Trinidadian food she grew up on — doubles, curry chicken roti, pholourie — out of a small Mid-City spot with a devoted following.

name: Praline Connection
tagline: Frenchmen Street soul food and Creole classics since 1990.
description: Fried chicken, smothered pork chops, stewed okra and file gumbo on Frenchmen Street, served by a staff in white shirts and black fedoras. A pre-show stop for decades of music crowds.

name: Boswell's Jamaican Grill
tagline: Jerk chicken and oxtail on Tulane Avenue.
description: A Jamaican kitchen on Tulane Avenue doing jerk chicken, curry goat, oxtail and festival — a straightforward counter that has held its regulars for years.

name: Ashé Cultural Arts Center
tagline: Central City's Black arts and community anchor on O.C. Haley.
description: Ashé programs theater, visual art, dance and community organizing out of Oretha Castle Haley Boulevard, and was central to the corridor's revival. Performance space, gallery, and meeting hall at once.

name: Studio Be
tagline: Brandan 'BMike' Odums' 35,000-square-foot mural warehouse in the Bywater.
description: BMike converted a Bywater warehouse into an immersive gallery of large-scale portraits of Black figures and movements. It reads as a museum and a mural at the same time, and there is nothing else like it in the city.

name: Le Musée de f.p.c.
tagline: A museum of the free people of color, in an Esplanade Avenue mansion.
description: Beverly McKenna's museum documents the history of New Orleans' free people of color through documents, art and furnishings held in a restored 1859 house on Esplanade. Guided tours only.

name: New Orleans African American Museum
tagline: Tremé museum on the campus of the historic Villa Meilleur.
description: Set in Tremé — the oldest Black neighborhood in the United States — NOAAM presents the art, history and culture of African Americans in New Orleans and the diaspora across a restored Creole villa and grounds.

name: Stella Jones Gallery
tagline: Contemporary fine art of the African diaspora, downtown.
description: Dr. Stella Jones has shown work by artists of African descent from across the diaspora since 1996, in a downtown gallery that operates at a national level rather than a local one.

name: Backstreet Cultural Museum
tagline: The Mardi Gras Indian and social aid & pleasure club archive in Tremé.
description: Founded by the late Sylvester Francis, Backstreet holds the largest collection of Mardi Gras Indian suits, second line regalia and jazz funeral documentation anywhere. A working community archive, not a curated exhibit.

name: Kermit's Tremé Mother-in-Law Lounge
tagline: Ernie K-Doe's bar, kept alive by Kermit Ruffins.
description: Ernie K-Doe opened it, Antoinette K-Doe kept it, and trumpeter Kermit Ruffins took it over. Live music, red beans off the grill out back, and a room painted in every color at once.

name: Sweet Lorraine's Jazz Club
tagline: St. Claude jazz room booking local players for local crowds.
description: A neighborhood jazz club on St. Claude Avenue that books New Orleans musicians for New Orleans audiences, away from the Frenchmen Street tourist circuit.

name: Zulu Social Aid & Pleasure Club
tagline: The Krewe of Zulu, parading since 1909.
description: Zulu is the oldest and best known Black carnival organization in New Orleans, whose Mardi Gras morning parade and hand-decorated coconuts are among the most sought-after traditions in the city. The North Broad clubhouse operates year round.

name: Sportsman's Corner
tagline: Central City corner bar and second line stop.
description: A Second Street corner bar that is a regular stop on the Central City second line routes — the kind of place where the parade comes to the door rather than passing by it.

name: Bullet's Sports Bar
tagline: Seventh Ward bar with live brass most nights of the week.
description: A neighborhood sports bar in the Seventh Ward that books real brass bands — Kermit Ruffins among the regulars — for a crowd that is almost entirely local.

name: Community Book Center
tagline: Bayou Road's Black bookstore and gathering place since 1983.
description: Vera Warren-Williams' bookstore on Bayou Road is as much a community living room as a shop — books by and about Black people, plus the meetings, readings and conversations that happen around them.

name: Baldwin & Co.
tagline: Bookstore, coffee bar and recording studio named for James Baldwin.
description: DJ Johnson built Baldwin & Co. on Elysian Fields as a bookstore with a café and a podcast studio in the back, programmed around Black writers and the conversations they start.

name: Deelightful Roux School of Cooking
tagline: Creole cooking classes from chef Dee Lavigne.
description: Chef Dee Lavigne teaches Creole cooking as history — gumbo, étouffée and the roux itself explained through the Black Creole lineage that produced them. Hands-on classes for small groups.
